transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
President Trump has issued an executive order requiring companies with federal contractors
to alert the White House and the agency they work for if lawmakers ask about their work
for the executive branch.
The White House says the order will help keep sensitive government information confidential.
The new rules could get an early test in January when Democrats regain control of Congress.
They're expected to launch investigations into members of the Trump administration.
President Trump is threatening to hit U.S. tech companies with what he calls a tremendous
tax.
NPR's Greg Myrie reports the president is taking a different approach when it comes
to selling American technology overseas.
Trump says he wants the U.S. to keep the lead in AI.
And he also said he won't allow U.S. companies to build AI data centers outside the U.S.
However, Trump is the one allowing Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China.
Nvidia's Jensen Wong lobbied Trump last year and persuaded the president to allow these
sales.
NPR's Greg Myrie reporting.
Ten years after voting to lead the European Union, the United Kingdom is taking what could
be a first step on the road to going back in.
Vicki Barker reports from London.
Over the next six months, negotiators will hammer out the details of Friday's landmark
agreement, granting British food and drink suppliers and Britain's young people easier
access to Europe.
Does that apply even if UK universities fail to meet an EU demand to lower tuition fees
for European students, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband telling the BBC?
It applies, and that's absolutely clear.
It's not so clear if you ask EU leaders, many of whom have children studying at UK universities.
A new poll finds a majority of Britons would now vote to rejoin the EU, and Miliband says
that may be on the table in the coming talks.
For NPR News, I'm Vicki Barker in London.
Artificial intelligence company Anthropic raised some money in the stock market this week.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the rest of the market suffered big losses, including the
tech-heavy Nasdaq.
Anthropic, which makes the popular AI chatbot Claude, raised tens of billions of dollars
with its initial public offering on Thursday.
The shares jumped about 17 percent in their first day of trading, and while they gave
up about half that gain on Friday, they still ended up for the week.
That was not the case for the broader market, which continues to be rattled by questions
about when or if the huge investment in artificial intelligence will pay off.
Some investors shifted money into bonds, pushing yields lower, but the average mortgage rate
was higher, at just over seven and a quarter percent.
For the week that Al lost eight percent, the S&P 500 index fell 8.6 percent, and the tech-heavy
Nasdaq tumbled 10 percent.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
This is NPR News in Washington.
A cyber attack has disrupted a U.S. Department of Agriculture system that sends payments
to farmers.
The USDA disclosed the attack on Friday.
Ryan Marquardt is vice president of the Iowa Farmers Union.
He says farmers have been expecting payments that never showed up.
It's really flabbergasting.
It's like, what is going on?
We shouldn't be left in the dark for five days while this system is down.
The USDA says the payment system had been affected since Monday.
The department says it expected most systems back online last night, and crews would work
through the weekend if needed.
Women are more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease than men, and PR's Ping Huang reports
new research suggests that changes during menopause may contribute.
In midlife, most women stop getting their periods.
The transition comes with fluctuating hormones, which affect parts of the brain involved in
memory.
Stephanie Perez, a researcher at the University of Texas at San Antonio, says in normal aging,
the brain compensates to spine.
But when you have these different genetic risk factors, not only for Alzheimer's disease,
but even for psychiatric illnesses, when you go through the transition, you're just more
at risk.
In mice, Perez and her colleagues found that a predisposition to Alzheimer's meant more
risk for cognitive decline.
They think it's related to hormonal changes, and are now looking into which ones and how
they affect risks.
She says current hormone replacement therapies, which tamp down on hot flashes, are not universally
helpful with cognitive deficits.
The research was presented at the Society for Neuroscience conference.
Ping Huang, NPR News.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Trump executive order requires federal contractors to alert White House when lawmakers ask questions
Trump threatens tremendous tax on U.S. tech companies while letting Nvidia sell advanced chips to China
UK takes first step toward rejoining the European Union with food, drink, and youth access agreement
Anthropic's stock jumps 17 percent in first day after IPO, but broader market slides sharply
Cyber attack disrupts USDA payment system, leaving farmers waiting on payments
New research suggests menopause hormonal changes may raise Alzheimer's risk in women, study finds
